blocks.text: The notice was pasted on the door at eye height, black on yellow, with the Tessary Works stamp in the corner: THIS STRUCTURE TO BE TAKEN DOWN ON THE FOURTH DAY FROM POSTING. It was posted on day fifteen.
Brisk patted the frame the way you'd pat a horse that had carried you a long way. "She's had a good innings."
"And the next door?" said Cressida.
Nobody had one.

Footnote: the door is the side door of the old Wool Hall on Fuller Street, south bank. It is the Bole's only south-side door to Ferrytown, distance two. The Ninefold's nine doors don't reach Ferrytown at all; Ferrytown re-hung its own Ninefold doors after a fire sixty-one years ago, and a changed frame is a dead frame for that pair. Ferrytown also has no bridge. Come out on its north bank and you queue for a ferry, then for customs, then for the rest of your afternoon. Every letter between our Exchange Desk and Ferrytown's goes through this frame, by runner.

Second footnote, because I can't help it: when a doorway is altered in either branch, it dies as a threshold for that pair. Every swap ever charged to the Ferrytown side of this frame becomes unsettleable on day nineteen, when the Works men take it out with crowbars. Settlement is rare. Rare is not never.
Before anyone took me anywhere, Cressida ran my hinge census.
"You're twenty-two," she said, at the Ninefold's west door, first from the left. "Old enough to have made one. Most people haven't. Your candidates."
I had written them out the night before, numbered, because I'd been nervous, and when I'm nervous I number things.
One. Sat the Survey entrance exam instead of taking the shorthand post at the River Board. Age nineteen.
Two. Told my mother I'd sat it, the same evening, before the results.
Three. Did not go to see my father in Weirside. Day zero.
Four. At seven, chose the dagger over the asterisk for my footnotes.
Cressida read the list once. She did not read number four aloud, which I appreciated, and did not comment on it, which I appreciated more.

A sounding is a reading that asks a question. You read a known route, then add the decision you suspect, the other way round, and if that branch exists the door warms under your palm. It opens nothing and spends nothing. Cressida laid her bare hand flat on the oak and read.
"The Bole. Ardent took the River Board post."
The wood stayed cold.
"The Bole. Ardent kept the exam from her mother."
Cold.
For the third she read Weirside's route first, my mother's hinge, then: "Ardent went to Sluice Row."
I watched her hand. I am not sure what I wanted. The door stayed exactly as cold as a door.
Footnote: so it was not heavy enough to split the world. It was heavy enough for me. Noted.

Cressida wrote a card in pinned ink. HINGE CENSUS. ARDENT, TR. Hinges: none. Mirrors: none. Under Shut branches she wrote nothing yet; that column fills from the Exchange Desk's ward-roll returns and takes about a week.
"Custom says never cross into your mirror," she said, blotting it.
"Is that in the Standing Orders, ma'am?"
"No. It's a superstition. Nobody has ever shown me a bill for it." She filed the card. "You have no mirror to stay out of. So it's academic. Next question?"
My next question was the door. My first, it turned out, was the lamplighter.

"Teague came by the desk yesterday," Cressida said, before I could ask. "Josiah. The rent landed on schedule, midnight ending day thirteen. Amos offered to go on to some other branch and pay his rent there instead." She squared the card drawer. "Josiah wouldn't have it. He said, better me than some other me."
I wrote that down in ordinary ink, which was the wrong ink, because it is a sentence I'd like to keep.
"I want to find the replacement door," I said. "Myself."
Cressida looked at me as if I'd handed her a figure with no units. "On what evidence?"
"The archive's, ma'am. A new door can't reach Ferrytown. It has to be older than both of Ferrytown's hinges, and unchanged on both sides. The archive will tell me which buildings are old enough."
"And it will tell you which frames are unchanged in Ferrytown?"
"No, ma'am. That can only be checked from inside."
"Then you have half a method," said Cressida. "Get the first half."
I spent the rest of day fifteen in the archive with the Ferrytown pin card at my elbow. Ferrytown has two hinges between it and us.
Hinge one: a hundred and thirty-nine years ago, Harbourmistress Ione Kember refused the Quay Charter.

Hinge two: ninety-seven years ago, the bridge vote. In the Bole, Alderman Prosper Hale cast the deciding vote for a bridge, and we got the high stone one with fourteen lamps a side. In Ferrytown he voted the other way, and they kept their ferries and built more.
So: a doorway built before the Quay Charter, still standing in the Bole, its frame never touched.

Before the bridge, the Bole had ferries too. Ferries need customs. The Bole's old ferry customs house still stands on the south landing, a squat stone box with a pillared porch, and the date over its door says it was raised a hundred and seventy-one years ago. Thirty-two years older than hinge one. Seventy-four years older than the bridge.

When the bridge opened, the Bole's ferries closed and the customs house became the River Board's paint store. I read every entry in the River Board's repair book for it, a hundred and two of them. Roof slates, four times. Windows, twice. A new lock. Never the frame. Never the step.

Footnote: I measured the Bole side myself at four in the afternoon, with the paint-store keeper watching me as if I might steal a tin of red lead. Width between jambs, thirty-eight and a quarter inches. Height to the lintel, seventy-nine and a half. A mason's mark on the left jamb at chest height, like a small wheel with a bar through it.
Cressida read my page and said, "Adequate." From Cressida, that is a hand on the shoulder.

"Brisk leads," she said. "Standing Order 6.3: a trainee may accompany any crew within the leader's licence, and Brisk's reaches distance eight. You go at dawn, through the Wool Hall door, while it still exists. I'll be at the Works office being unpleasant about a four-day notice."
That night I made my ballast.

The Book says a ballast is a trivial fact you make by an act, in your native branch, and that a witness spoils it. The first bill is paid in full. I had paid mine; the word Linnet still sat on line one of that first bill, in my own hand, meaning nothing to me. The second bill I intended to pay in something cheaper.

I made it in my room on Weir Lane, door shut, lamp out, with my back to the window in case the window counted. My mother called up the stairs, "Sabeth, there's soup," and I said, "One minute," and finished, and went down, and ate the soup, and did not think about it, which is harder than it sounds.

It's spent now, so I can tell you the kind: a private knot. I tied it blind, inside the lining of my left cuff, to a design I made up on the spot and will not describe even now, on principle. I did not look at it afterwards. The Book says looking at your own ballast doesn't count. I still didn't look.
It would settle at the seventh midnight after I tied it, the midnight ending day twenty-two. We were crossing on day sixteen. Fresh as bread.
Day sixteen, dawn, the Wool Hall door.

Brisk turned out her pockets on the step before anything else. Pilot's habit. A pencil. Two coins. A tin of mints. No bridge-company toll chit, no penny with the bridge stamped on it, nothing that needs a bridge to make sense.
"Ferrytown's never had one," she said. "Carry a bridge in your pocket and she'll take that first. Glare." She put the coins back. "Your bill, Ardent."

My Form 9 was in my breast pocket, in pinned ink. Line one: My given name is Sabeth. I had written it because I would hate to lose that one too, which surprised me. Shorthand at ninety words a minute. My mother teaching me the bowline. Wants Chainman. Cannot swim. Dagger footnotes since seven.
Brisk stood in the doorway and read the Bole side's route. Two hinges. Kember's charter, refused. Hale's bridge, unbuilt.
The air went cool and wet and smelled of tar.
"Door's open," said Brisk. "Nine. Eight. Move, people."
I moved. That was the Bole's opening to Ferrytown spent for the day, every door, gone at a word. Entering costs nothing. Leaving is where they get you.
On the Ferrytown side, the Wool Hall is a ferry company's booking hall, and the clerk at the counter didn't look up. We walked out onto Fuller Street.
Ferrytown has no bridge.

I knew that from the card. Knowing it from the card is not the same as standing on Fuller Street with the river in front of you and nothing over it. Where our bridge marches across on its fourteen lamps, Ferrytown has water, and on the water, everything. Flat ferries for carts. Skiffs for people. A ferry with a brass bell for the post. Every landing has a bell, and every bell has an opinion. The noise is enormous and nobody seems to notice it.
Footnote: I cannot swim. I noticed the water.

The customs house stood on the south landing exactly where ours stands. Same squat stone box. Same pillared porch. In Ferrytown it is not a paint store. It is a customs house, open and busy, with a queue of carters out the door and an officer in a blue coat stamping manifests at a table in the porch.
"She's still working," said Brisk, delighted. "Look at her."

We measured it while the queue complained about us. Width between jambs: thirty-eight and a quarter. Height to the lintel: seventy-nine and a half. Mason's mark on the left jamb at chest height, a small wheel with a bar through it. Same step, with the same worn dip where a hundred and seventy-one years of boots have come in.
I wrote it all down twice. My hand did not shake. My hand doesn't, as a rule. It is the rest of me that does.

On the way down the steps, a carter's barrow caught Brisk's kit roll. It came undone, and everything in it went down the steps: pencils, a measuring tape, a folded oilskin, and a small tin that hit the bottom step and sprang its lid.
A pebble rolled out of the tin. I picked it up to hand it back.
It was smooth and grey, and someone had scratched a mark into one face with a nail. I saw the mark. I didn't mean to. I turned it over to see which way to give it to her, and I saw it.
Brisk looked at the pebble in my hand. I looked at it. The carter said sorry and went on.
"Ah," said Brisk. "Well. That's that, then."

Footnote: a witness is a support. Something in the world now agreed with Brisk's ballast, and the something was me. It was spoiled the moment I saw it, and ballast can only be made in your native branch, so she couldn't make another here. She hadn't brought a spare. Nobody brings a spare for a day trip to distance two. That sentence is going in my notes until I die.
I stood on the steps of the Ferrytown customs house and did what I do when I am frightened. I ran Least Agreement for Brisk.
One. Hinge fact. Ferrytown split from us by other people's decisions, long before Brisk was born. It isn't on the other side of any hinge of hers. Nothing.

Two. Glare. She'd turned out her pockets at the Wool Hall. No toll chit. No bridge penny. Nothing she carried needed anything Ferrytown lacks. Decoy glare is licensed to Seconds, and Brisk is a Second, but only for the six objects on the inert list, and the inert kit lives in a locked case in the Hall. Nothing.
Three. Ballast. Spoiled. By me.
Four. Orphans: the oldest fact she has that nothing in Ferrytown supports.
"Don't put my birthday in your sums, Ardent," said Brisk, reading over my shoulder.
I didn't. I don't know her birthday. I put a question mark beside it, and she said, "Leave it," so I left it.

Her first memory is being carried over the Tessary bridge, counting its lamps. She told it at the lamps during the Teague case, and I wrote it down because I write everything down. Ferrytown has no bridge and no lamps over the water. Nothing in this branch supports that memory, and it is very old. Nothing else of hers that I knew of was as old.
Five. Strays. We never got to five.
"So it's the bridge," said Brisk.
"It's the bridge."
She looked out at all that water with nothing over it. "Fourteen lamps," she said. "I'd have liked to keep counting them."
"I'm sorry," I said. "I picked it up."

"Barrow's fault. Steps' fault. My tin's fault, it's had a loose lid since spring." She wrapped the spoiled pebble in a handkerchief, as if it were still worth something, and put it in her pocket. "Bill's a bill, Ardent. Come on. We've a hall to visit."

Ferrytown's Survey keeps its hall on the south bank above the ferry stairs. Their Verity Sallis was leaning in the doorframe of the threshold room with her whole shoulder, as if doorframes were furniture.

It is a disconcerting thing, to see our Verity's face doing that. Ours keeps an arm's length from every frame in the Ninefold. This one had her sleeves rolled to the elbow, ink to the wrist, and a sunburn.
"You're the Bole's," she said, cheerful. "I can always tell. You look at our river like it's missing something."
"It is," I said. "Ma'am."
"Not a ma'am. Field cartographer. I draw the streets. I'm across most days, somewhere or other." She slapped the frame beside her, fondly. "How's my other? Still doing it all from a desk?"
"She works the Least-Agreement Tables," I said. "From the desk. She's right four times in five."

"She would be." Verity grinned. "I write to her every quarter. She answers in tables." She looked at Brisk's face, then at mine, and the grin went somewhere more careful. "Someone's paid for something."
Brisk told her about the steps. Verity was kind about it, quickly, and then sent a boy to their Exchange Desk.
"Desk hasn't read to the Bole today," she said. "I've told them not to. Ferrytown's side is yours. Read it wherever you like."

We filed our measurements with Ferrytown's Survey. They copied them into their own pin book, because their customs house was about to become a door to the Bole whether their customs officers liked it or not.
While they copied, Verity leaned on the frame again and said, "You know the Bole keeps a file on her? On my other."
"I didn't know that."
"There's always a file. I asked your desk for a copy once. I like to know my counterparts." She said it lightly. "Kittering Lane. Pin died during a family visit. Your lot filed it natural decay."

I wrote down Kittering Lane. I wrote down pin died during a family visit. I did not write down that our Verity has never once, in my sight, touched a doorframe. I didn't need to write that down. I already knew it.
Footnote: natural decay is a stamp. I have seen a lot of that stamp lately.
She walked us back to the customs house at dusk. The queue had gone home. The officer in the blue coat let us stand in his doorway on Verity's word and our promise not to stamp anything.
Brisk stood in the frame. I stood behind her with the Ferrytown pin card and my pen, because a door you have found and dated and measured is still nothing until it opens.
Brisk read Ferrytown's side. Kember's charter, refused. Hale's bridge, unbuilt.
It opened on the first reading.
Paint and turpentine and the cold of a shut room in the Bole came through the frame, and beyond it, in the last of the light, tins of red lead along a shelf.
That is a long threshold. A hundred and seventy-one years old, unchanged on both sides, older than both hinges. Proved.
"Nine," said Brisk. "Eight."

I wrote it on the card in shorthand, the one thing I can do faster than Brisk can count. Customs house, south landing, front door. Long threshold. Opens from Ferrytown side, first reading, day sixteen. Ardent, Tr., for Brisk to countersign.
"Seven. Move, people."

We moved. On the way through, the doorway took its fee. I felt a small tug, nothing I could name. The lining of my left cuff had nothing in it. Somewhere behind me, Ferrytown's Ardent now had a knot she never tied, and had lost nothing for it.
Footnote: that is the whole of a ballasted crossing. A tug. A knot. Kind logged: private knot, Ferrytown, spent.
"Six," said Brisk, and stepped through after me, last out, as pilots are.
Standing Order 9.1: read your bill at the threshold. She unfolded hers in the doorway, with the Ferrytown lanterns behind her, and read it by their light.
"Five."
Her finger stopped on a line. I watched her read it twice.

"Huh," said Brisk. "Says I was carried over the Tessary bridge, counting its lamps." She looked at me. "I wasn't. I was carried onto a ferry. Counting its lanterns. Somebody said good girl." She folded the bill along its old crease. "Same somebody, I reckon. Four."

Footnote: and on the far side of this frame, Ferrytown's Brisk now remembers being carried over a bridge her world never built, counting fourteen lamps that were never lit there. If she ever goes looking for it, there will be nothing along that bank but water. I would like that on the record.
"Three."

Second footnote. From that crossing on, I treated ballast as a craft and not a chore. One: designs no witness can spoil; nothing that rolls, nothing that shows. Two: batches made in the Bole and timed to be fresh on the day, with spares, always spares, even for distance two. Three: a running ledger of every kind I spend, branch by branch, in pinned ink, because thirty-one is all there is and I intend to know where each one went.
"Two."
Behind Brisk, on the Ferrytown step, their Verity had come right up to the frame. She put her hand flat on the jamb, by the little wheel, as easily as on a banister.

"One," said Brisk, and on the ninth breath Ferrytown's Verity leaned to the closing door and called through it: "Is she still pretending she's scared of doors? Ask her what happened in Kittering Lane when she was nine."
